summary: Describes how SIP is used for subscriptions and notifications about presence, meaning a person's willingness and ability to communicate. It goes beyond simple online and offline flags to support richer status information.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3856 defines how SIP users subscribe to updates about another user's presence. A presence agent checks the request and sends updates when the presence information changes.

questions: how does sip subscribe and notify work
subtitle: How SIP subscriptions and notifications let users receive updates about another user's presence.

tldr.problem: Communication systems need to share whether a user is willing and able to communicate, including more information than a simple online or offline state.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a SIP event package named presence. A watcher subscribes to a presence agent, which authenticates and authorizes the request and sends NOTIFY messages with presence information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3856 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8996. It defines a SIP event package that is also compliant with the Common Presence Profile framework.

facts.label: Recommended notification rate
facts.value: No more than once every five seconds per presentity

today: RFC 3856 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Presence Information over SIP
sections.content:
Presence describes a user's ability and willingness to communicate across devices. The RFC uses SIP's event notification framework to let interested parties, called watchers, subscribe to that information and receive updates.

A logical entity called a presence agent accepts subscriptions, stores their state and sends notifications when presence changes. SIP networks can route these requests to the server that holds a user's registration state. The event package is also designed to interwork with systems that follow the Common Presence Profile.
sections.plainLanguage: Presence describes whether and how a user can communicate. SIP lets another user ask for this information and receive updates from a presence agent.

sections.title: A Subscription and Its Updates
sections.content:
A watcher sends a SUBSCRIBE request that identifies the person, or presentity, whose presence it wants to learn. The presence agent authenticates the request and then checks whether the presentity has authorized it. A successful decision returns 200; a pending decision returns 202. In either case, the agent sends an immediate NOTIFY.

The subscription creates a SIP dialog, which holds the state needed for further messages. The subscriber refreshes the subscription before it expires. Sending a SUBSCRIBE with an Expires value of zero ends the subscription and can also request a one-time update of current presence.
sections.plainLanguage: A watcher requests another person's presence, and the presence agent checks the request. The agent sends an initial update and later sends more when the information changes.

sections.title: Naming a Presentity
sections.content:
A presentity can be identified with a SIP URI, a SIPS URI or a protocol-independent pres URI such as pres:user@domain. A server maps a pres URI to a protocol-specific address.

If a subscriber knows both a valid pres URI and a SIP or SIPS URI, the RFC says it should use the pres URI. This can help gateways connect SIP presence to other systems that follow the Common Presence Profile. A pres URI may fail where a proxy does not understand that URI scheme, so the recommendation is not mandatory.
sections.plainLanguage: A pres URI names a person without choosing a particular messaging protocol. When the subscriber knows a valid pres URI, the RFC recommends using it so other compatible systems can handle the identity.

sections.title: The Presence Event Package
sections.content:
The event package name is presence, carried in the Event header of SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY requests. A SUBSCRIBE normally has no body; it may include a filter asking for only certain events or information, but this RFC does not define filter documents.

The default subscription duration is 3600 seconds, though a subscriber may request another value. NOTIFY messages carry a presence document. All subscribers and notifiers must support application/pidf+xml, which is also the default when the SUBSCRIBE has no Accept header.
sections.plainLanguage: A presence subscription normally lasts 3600 seconds unless the subscriber requests another duration. The agent sends presence documents in a format that both sides must support.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
A presence agent must authenticate every subscription before deciding whether to authorize it. The RFC requires support for Digest authentication. Authentication identifies the requester; authorization determines whether the presentity has allowed that requester to receive presence information.

The agent must not accept a subscription without authorization from the presentity. It reports the decision as successful (200), rejected (403 or 603) or pending (202). In a technique called polite blocking, the agent may return 200 while sending a notification that does not reveal that the request was blocked.
sections.plainLanguage: The presence agent must check who is asking and whether the presentity has authorized the request. It reports the result as successful, rejected or pending.

sections.title: Sending and Reading Notifications
sections.content:
A presence agent may send a NOTIFY at any time, usually when the presentity's state changes. A notification normally contains the complete current presence state. Within one dialog, the document in the NOTIFY with the highest CSeq is current; if that message has no document, the next-highest CSeq document is used.

A presence agent should not send updates for one presentity more than once every five seconds. If a pending request is later authorized, the agent should send a notification. The RFC allows notifications to be signed or encrypted with S/MIME.
sections.plainLanguage: Notifications usually contain the full current presence state, and the newest document takes priority. The agent should not send updates for one person more than once every five seconds.

sections.title: Protecting Presence Information
sections.content:
The RFC treats presence as highly sensitive. TLS can encrypt each network connection, but this hop-by-hop protection lets proxies see message contents. S/MIME can provide end-to-end encryption or message integrity, though it does not hide all information or prevent traffic analysis.

Attackers could forge or replay an old presence document, or use subscriptions to generate unwanted traffic. The RFC requires authentication and authorization, describes timestamps for detecting replayed documents when S/MIME signatures are used, and points to controls for removing unwanted subscriptions and limiting request floods.
sections.plainLanguage: Presence can reveal private information, so the agent checks subscriptions and systems can encrypt or sign messages. Timestamps and subscription controls help address replay and unwanted notification attacks.
